quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "could" and the /j/ starting "yield" don't survive as separate sounds in fast speech. What do they turn into together?
quests.explanation: This is why "could yield" doesn't sound like two crisp, separate words: the boundary consonant /d/ and the /j/ of "yield" merge into the single sound /dʒ/.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the /d/ at the end of "second". With another consonant right before it and another right after (from "language"), can a speaker realistically hit all three cleanly?
quests.explanation: This is elision: a sound is removed entirely, not changed or weakened. Here, the /d/ at the end of "second" disappears before the consonant that starts "language".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "seven cars" at natural speed. Listen right at the boundary — does the /n/ stay a /n/, or does it become something else?
quests.explanation: This is regressive assimilation: a sound changes to become more like the sound that follows it. Here, the /n/ ending "seven" turns into /ŋ/ because "cars" begins with a velar consonant.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A bilabial consonant is coming up in "buy". What does that do to the /d/ just before it in "good"?
quests.explanation: Speakers save effort by letting /d/ anticipate the bilabial sound ahead. So in "good buy", /d/ is pronounced as /b/ instead.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try saying "plant trees" at a natural conversational pace, not word by word. What happens to the /t/ sound in the middle?
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely pronounce every consonant in a heavy cluster. In "plant trees", the /t/ is left out completely, letting the surrounding consonants connect directly.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Notice how the mouth has to move from the /n/ ending "ten" to the velar sound that opens "coupons". Does it really make that full move, or take a shortcut?
quests.explanation: Unlike elision, nothing is dropped here — the sound simply changes place. /n/ becomes /ŋ/ in "ten coupons" to match the velar consonant that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a spelling trap: "Africa" looks like it should flow straight into "is", but a sound gets inserted that isn't written anywhere. Can you hear it?
quests.explanation: Since "Africa" doesn't end in a written consonant that could explain a /r/, the /r/ you hear before "is" is added by the speech system itself — an intrusive sound, not a spelled one.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a sound-merging boundary. What new consonant replaces /t/ + /j/ when you say "won't yield" naturally?
quests.explanation: Coalescence is a genuine sound change, not just fast talking — /t/ plus /j/ reliably becomes /tʃ/ in phrases like "won't yield" across natural English speech.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Three consonants in a row is hard work for the mouth. Focus on the /t/ where "contact" meets "number" — does English keep it or drop it?
quests.explanation: Because /t/ is squeezed between two other consonants, it gets dropped in fluent speech. Say "contact number" aloud and you'll notice the /t/ just isn't there.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two vowels back to back is awkward to say smoothly. What sound does natural speech add between "drama" and "award" — despite it not appearing in either word's spelling?
quests.explanation: This is a purely phonetic addition: /r/ shows up between "drama" and "award" only to ease pronunciation, with nothing in either word's spelling to account for it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Nothing in "idea"'s ending suggests a consonant at all. So the /r/ you might hear before "of" isn't really part of either word — where does it come from?
quests.explanation: Vowel hiatus (two vowels in a row) is uncomfortable in fluent English, so an intrusive /r/ fills the gap in "idea of" — a sound created by the flow of speech, not by spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In casual speech, does the final /t/ of "kept" get pronounced before "quiet", or does it just vanish?
quests.explanation: English speakers simplify clusters like this one by deleting a stop consonant rather than forcing it in. The /t/ in "kept" is the one that goes missing before "quiet".
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Picture how a native speaker would say "fast lane" in a fast, everyday sentence. Is every single consonant still there?
quests.explanation: This is a textbook case of consonant-cluster elision: the /t/ between two consonants is dropped to keep speech fluent and effortless in "fast lane".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try blending "good" straight into "yield" without a pause. The /d/ and /j/ fuse — into what sound?
quests.explanation: The two sounds don't just sit next to each other; they blend into /dʒ/. That's the defining feature of coalescence, and it's exactly what happens in "good yield".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the consonant joining "send" to "back". Is it still /d/, or has it changed shape to match what follows?
quests.explanation: When a word ending in /d/ meets a bilabial sound, the /d/ shifts to /b/ so both sounds are made in nearly the same place in the mouth. That's what happens in "send back".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Check the spelling: "more" ends in 'r'. Before a consonant or pause it usually stays silent — so what happens before the vowel starting "or"?
quests.explanation: The final 'r' in "more" behaves like a switch: silent before consonants, audible before vowels. Since "or" starts with a vowel, the /r/ links the two words together smoothly.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In connected speech, the /t/ ending "set" often adapts to its neighbor. What does it turn into right before the velar sound in "goal"?
quests.explanation: This is place assimilation: /t/ moves to a velar position to blend smoothly with what comes next, turning into /k/ in "set goal".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "bless" ends in /s/ and "you" begins with a /j/ sound. What single new consonant do the two combine into?
quests.explanation: When /s/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two often fuse into a single new consonant. In "bless you", /s/ + /j/ becomes /ʃ/ — a completely different sound from either original.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Instead of hearing /t/ and /j/ separately between "last" and "year", listen for one fused sound. What is it?
quests.explanation: This is coalescent assimilation: two adjacent sounds merge into a third sound that resembles neither one alone. Here, /t/ and /j/ combine into /tʃ/ in "last year".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /d/ in "hard" is trapped between two other consonants right before "luck". What usually happens to a stop consonant stuck in that position?
quests.explanation: Rather than pronounce all three consonants back to back, speakers cut the /d/ from "hard" entirely. The result flows straight from the first consonant into "luck".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "what". With a bilabial consonant starting "month" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /t/ ending "what" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /t/ becomes /p/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "month".
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "great band" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /t/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /t/ rarely stays /t/ before a bilabial sound — it assimilates to /p/, which is exactly what you hear in "great band".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "soda" has no letter for /r/ anywhere at its end. So if you hear a /r/ before "and", where does it actually come from?
quests.explanation: English avoids putting two vowel sounds directly next to each other, so speakers insert a small linking sound to bridge them. Since "soda" has no /r/ in its spelling, this /r/ is intrusive — added purely for smoothness, not because it's really part of "soda" or "and".
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The tongue is already anticipating "park"'s bilabial sound before it even finishes "green". What happens to /n/ as a result?
quests.explanation: The change from /n/ to /m/ at the end of "green" happens because the following bilabial consonant in "park" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "wide" and "collar" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /d/ ending "wide" adopts the velar quality of the sound in "collar", surfacing as /g/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The 'r' in "before" isn't always pronounced. Does the vowel at the start of "anyone" bring it back to life?
quests.explanation: Because the letter 'r' genuinely exists at the end of "before", its reappearance before the vowel in "anyone" is called linking /r/ — a real, spelled sound resurfacing, unlike intrusive /r/, which comes from nowhere in the spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "bad year" quickly and casually. The /d/ and the /j/ in "year" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /d/ and /j/ into /dʒ/. That's why "bad year" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant collision at the boundary of "want" and "your": /t/ meets /j/. Which single sound comes out the other side?
quests.explanation: Coalescence happens when neighboring sounds are so close in the mouth that they collapse into one. /t/ and /j/ become /tʃ/ in "want your" — faster and easier to say than keeping the two sounds apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen closely at the boundary of "point" and "taken" — count the consonants stacking up. Does the /t/ still make it into the sentence?
quests.explanation: In fast, connected speech, a /t/ wedged between consonants almost always disappears. That's what you'll hear in "point taken" — the /t/ goes silent.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two consonants become one here. Focus on where "wouldn't" ends and "you" begins — what's the resulting blended sound?
quests.explanation: This merge is extremely common wherever a word ending in /t/ meets a "you"-type word. In "wouldn't you", the result is /tʃ/, not /t/ followed by /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.
